content:
iVerify today released a report detailing P7 DarkSword, a new variant of the DarkSword iPhone exploit chain malware exposed earlier this year. Details below.

A little background

Earlier this year, Google and iVerify uncovered two sophisticated iPhone hacking tools, named Coruna and DarkSword respectively, both of which chained multiple iOS vulnerabilities to compromise devices running older versions of the system.

In the case of DarkSword, once an iPhone is compromised, the attacker can deploy additional malware to access sensitive data.

Coruna targets devices running iOS 13 through iOS 17.2.1, while DarkSword affects iPhones running iOS 18.4 through iOS 18.7.

Apple subsequently rolled out system updates for the affected older iOS versions, including iOS 15.8.7, iOS 16.7.15, and iOS 18.7.7. Apple also made the unprecedented move of offering iOS 18.7.7 to devices capable of installing iOS 26, ensuring that users who chose not to upgrade to the latest system version would also receive protection against DarkSword.

At the time, Google stated that DarkSword was being used by multiple commercial spyware vendors and was suspected of involving nation-state actors, with victims located in Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine.

New DarkSword variant discovered in the wild

iVerify today announced the discovery of P7 DarkSword, a previously unseen variant found during its investigation two months ago into the infection of an iPhone belonging to an employee of a financial institution.

According to information provided by iVerify to 9to5Mac, P7 extends compatibility from iOS 18.6, the version tracked in earlier variants, to iOS 18.7. Other DarkSword deployments observed by Google had in fact already supported iOS 18.7.

The company also indicated that the threat actors behind P7 are distributing it through malicious advertising as part of watering hole attacks — meaning victims are not necessarily individually targeted. Users who simply encounter malicious or compromised web content may fall victim as part of a larger-scale attack campaign.

The full report states:

"In August 2026, we investigated a DarkSword infection and discovered it to be a previously unseen variant, which we have named P7 DarkSword. The name P7 derives from the fact that the threat actors used the p7_ variable prefix when modifying the original DarkSword code. Compared to the variants we typically observe, P7 has reduced its on-device footprint, added capabilities to steal Keychain data and cryptocurrency wallets, and introduced two-way C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure. This article will describe the investigation process, the variant's capabilities, and indicators available for detection."

The report notes that P7 DarkSword advances beyond previous variants in three main areas: stealth, stability, and functionality. The new variant reduces the number of logging and process injection operations, leverages browser storage to avoid re-infecting the same device, and expands data theft capabilities.

iVerify also told 9to5Mac that these changes appear to be the result of significant effort by the operators, rather than merely AI-assisted modifications. The company noted that P7 is more capable of concealing itself and cleaning up after its activities, rendering previous indicators of compromise (IOCs) obsolete.

Most notably, iVerify stated that P7 can directly extract Keychain data on the iPhone and transmit it to the attacker, rather than copying the entire Keychain database for processing elsewhere.

P7 DarkSword can also target cryptocurrency wallet data and introduces a more advanced two-way communication mechanism to interface with the attacker's command-and-control infrastructure.

This two-way communication also gives the attacker greater control over compromised devices. According to iVerify, P7 can receive commands to retrieve arbitrary files, upload photos, enumerate installed applications, access the Apple Notes database, collect data from individual app containers, and scan the device's file system.

By default, the spyware queries the attacker's command-and-control server for new commands every 15 seconds, although this interval can be changed remotely.

It is worth noting that P7 itself is not a new iOS vulnerability, but rather a new version of malware deployed after a successful compromise via DarkSword. iVerify did not disclose which version of iOS the device discovered to be running P7 in August was using.
